en: Agreement or harmony; a formal treaty; to give or grant
hook: ACCORD: hearts (cor) in agreement.
story: Accord. Two families near Comilla had quarrelled for years over a narrow strip of land between their fields. Finally, the elders brought them together under the banyan tree. After hours of talk, both sides agreed to share the strip as a footpath. They had reached an accord: an agreement, a state of harmony. An accord can also be a formal treaty, like a peace accord. As a verb, to accord means to give or grant, as in according someone respect. Synonyms: agreement, pact.

gre.s: After decades of hostility, the two neighboring states finally reached a historic ____ on sharing the river's waters, though skeptics doubted it would survive the next drought.
gre.clue: though skeptics doubted it would survive the next drought

en: To stick firmly; to follow a rule or belief
hook: ADHERE: like ADHESIVE tape.
story: Adhere. Before every exam, Priya's hostel puts up a notice: phones off and lights out by eleven. Most of the girls ignore it. Priya adheres to it strictly, every single night, and her roommates tease her for it. To adhere is to follow a rule or belief faithfully. Its first meaning is physical: to stick firmly, the way a stamp adheres to an envelope. Adhesive tape sticks to paper; an adherent sticks to a cause. Synonyms: stick, abide, comply.

gre.s: Although the committee claimed to ____ to the principle of transparency, it conducted most of its deliberations behind closed doors and published no minutes.
gre.clue: it conducted most of its deliberations behind closed doors

en: Created for a particular purpose only, not planned in advance
hook: AD HOC: Latin for 'for this' — for this one purpose only.
story: Ad hoc. When floodwater suddenly poured into the ground floor of a hospital in Sylhet, there was no plan for it. Doctors, cleaners, and patients' relatives formed an ad hoc team on the spot, passing beds and medicine boxes upstairs in a human chain. Ad hoc means created for one particular purpose only, not planned in advance. The Latin literally means for this. An ad hoc committee dissolves when its task is done. Contrast systematic. Synonyms: improvised, impromptu, makeshift.

gre.s: Rather than developing a coherent policy, the ministry responded to each crisis in a purely ____ fashion, devising quick fixes that were abandoned once the emergency passed.
gre.clue: Rather than developing a coherent policy

en: Including everything
hook: ALL-ENCOMPASSING: a COMPASS that circles everything.
story: All-encompassing. When Rafi's grandfather began writing a history of their village, he did not stop at the important families. He recorded every pond, every mosque and temple, every flood since 1950, even the names of cows and the recipes for festival sweets. His notebook was all-encompassing: including absolutely everything. To encompass is to surround or include, as if drawing a circle with a compass around it all. An all-encompassing grief fills every corner of life. Synonyms: comprehensive, exhaustive, universal.

gre.s: Far from the narrow survey its modest title suggested, the study was nearly ____, covering every aspect of the region's economy from river fishing to software.
gre.clue: covering every aspect of the region's economy

en: A short, wise statement of a general truth
hook: APHORISM: a short AFFIRMATION of truth.
story: Aphorism. Mitu's grandmother rarely gave long lectures. Instead, she offered short, wise sentences that stuck forever. "An empty pitcher makes the most noise." "The branch heavy with fruit bends low." Years later, Mitu still quotes them at the office. These were aphorisms: short, wise statements of a general truth. The word comes from the Greek for marking a boundary, the same root as horizon; an aphorism draws a sharp line around a truth. Synonyms: maxim, adage, proverb.

gre.s: The essay closes with a single pithy ____, "Certainty ages a face faster than doubt," which has been quoted far more often than any of the arguments that precede it.
gre.clue: a single pithy

en: A standard against which things are measured
hook: BENCHMARK: a mark on the workbench to measure against.
story: Benchmark. When Tanvir joined a running club in Ramna Park, the coach timed him over five kilometres: thirty-four minutes. That number became his benchmark, the standard against which every later run was measured. Three months later, he finished in twenty-seven. A benchmark is a standard or point of reference for comparison. Originally, surveyors cut a mark into stone to rest their levelling bench on. Companies benchmark their products against rivals. Synonyms: standard, yardstick, touchstone.

gre.s: For decades, the textbook's rigorous treatment of the subject served as the ____ against which all later introductions were judged, and few of them measured up.
gre.clue: against which all later introductions were judged

en: Damaged or spoiled; suffering from decay
hook: BLIGHT: a plant disease that withers crops.
story: Blighted. One monsoon, a fungus crept across the rice fields of Babu's uncle in Dinajpur. Within two weeks, the green stalks had turned brown and withered. The crop was blighted: damaged and spoiled, struck by disease or decay. A neighbourhood can be blighted too, with empty buildings, broken windows, and heaps of rubbish. A blight is anything that spoils or ruins, as the potato blight ruined Ireland's harvests in the 1840s. Synonyms: ruined, spoiled, devastated.

gre.s: Once a thriving industrial district, the riverside neighborhood is now ____, its factories abandoned and its streets lined with crumbling, boarded-up houses.
gre.clue: its factories abandoned and its streets lined with crumbling, boarded-up houses

en: Peacefully satisfied
hook: CON-TENT (stress on TENT): happy in your little tent.
story: Content. Rahim, a boatman on the Meghna, owns one wooden boat, a tin-roofed house, and three goats. Each evening he sits by the river with a cup of tea and watches the sunset. When a visitor from the city asked whether he wanted more, he laughed. "What more? I have enough." He is content: peacefully satisfied with what he has. Stress the second syllable, con-TENT. Do not confuse it with CON-tent, what something contains. Synonyms: satisfied, serene.

gre.s: Unlike her restless siblings, who constantly chased new ventures, she was ____ with the quiet life of a village schoolteacher and never sought promotion.
gre.clue: Unlike her restless siblings, who constantly chased new ventures

en: Reduced in quality, value, or moral character
hook: DE-BASED: brought to a BASE (low) level.
story: Debased. Long ago, rulers sometimes mixed cheap copper into their silver coins so they could mint more of them. The coins looked the same, but each one was worth less. The currency had been debased: lowered in quality and value. A person can be debased too, morally degraded, and a word can be debased through overuse; think of how awesome now describes a sandwich. De means down: brought down to a baser level. Synonyms: degraded, corrupted, cheapened.

gre.s: Critics lamented that the once-dignified art of political debate had become ____, reduced to an exchange of personal insults and slogans crafted for television.
gre.clue: reduced to an exchange of personal insults

en: Causing one to feel unsettled or uneasy
hook: DIS-CONCERT-ING: throws the CONCERT out of tune.
story: Disconcerting. During her visa interview, Ishita answered every question carefully. The officer said nothing. He simply stared at her file and kept writing for two full minutes without looking up. The silence was disconcerting: it made her feel unsettled and uneasy. A painting whose eyes seem to follow you around the room is disconcerting too. Concert suggests harmony, and dis breaks it: something disconcerting throws you out of tune. Synonyms: unsettling, unnerving, disquieting.

gre.s: Audiences found the film's abrupt shifts in tone ____: scenes of broad slapstick gave way, without warning, to moments of genuine brutality.
gre.clue: gave way, without warning, to moments of genuine brutality

en: Still in existence
hook: EXTANT: still standing, not EXTINCT.
story: Extant. Thousands of terracotta plaques once covered the walls of the Kantajew temple in Dinajpur. An earthquake in 1897 toppled its towers, and over the years some plaques were stolen. Thankfully, most are still extant: still in existence, surviving today. Historians love this word. Of the more than one hundred plays the Greek writer Sophocles wrote, only seven are extant. Do not confuse it with extinct, its opposite, meaning gone forever. Synonyms: surviving, existing, remaining.

gre.s: Although the playwright is known to have written more than forty comedies, only three are ____ today; the rest perished when the theater's archives burned.
gre.clue: the rest perished

en: Natural ease or skill in doing something
hook: GRE trick: FACILITY means ease — she has a facility for languages.
story: Facility. Joya's little brother has never taken a single music lesson, yet he can hear a song once on the radio and play it on the harmonium straight away. His teachers are amazed by his facility with melody: a natural ease and skill in doing something. The word is related to facile and facilitate, all from the Latin for easy. Facility also means a building, like a sports facility, but the GRE prefers the ease sense. Synonyms: aptitude, fluency, knack.

gre.s: Despite her obvious ____ with languages, which allowed her to pick up conversational Italian in a matter of weeks, she struggled for years with basic arithmetic.
gre.clue: pick up conversational Italian in a matter of weeks

en: Active or occurring in irregular bursts; not steady
hook: FITFUL: in FITS and starts.
story: Fitful. On the night before her GRE, Rumana's sleep was fitful. She drifted off, woke at one, dozed again, woke at three to check the alarm, then lay staring at the ceiling until dawn. Her sleep came in irregular bursts, never steady. Fitful means occurring in irregular bursts, stopping and starting. Think of the phrase fits and starts. A fitful wind gusts and then dies; fitful progress lurches forward, then stalls. Synonyms: intermittent, sporadic, erratic.

gre.s: Progress on the bridge has been ____ at best, with long stretches of inactivity interrupted by brief bursts of construction whenever funds arrived.
gre.clue: long stretches of inactivity interrupted by brief bursts

en: To encourage or stir up violent or unlawful behavior
hook: INCITE: light a fire INSIDE the crowd.
story: Incite. A fake video spread online claiming that a factory had poisoned the local river. Within hours, a man with a megaphone was shouting outside the factory gates, urging the crowd to break in and burn the warehouse. Police later charged him with inciting violence: stirring up and encouraging unlawful behaviour. Incite and excite share a root meaning to set in motion, but you incite people to do something, usually something bad. Synonyms: provoke, instigate, foment.

gre.s: Prosecutors argued that the pamphlets were written not merely to criticize the government but to ____ riots, pointing to passages that urged readers to burn public buildings.
gre.clue: urged readers to burn public buildings

en: To persuade; to bring about or cause
hook: INDUCE: lead (duce) INTO.
story: Induce. Arif's grandmother had not slept properly for a week, so the doctor gave her a mild medicine to induce sleep: to bring it about. Meanwhile, Arif was trying to induce her to stop drinking six cups of strong tea after sunset: to persuade her. Induce means to persuade someone, or to cause something to happen. In means into, and duc means lead: to lead someone into an action or a state. Synonyms: persuade, prompt, cause.

gre.s: No amount of flattery could ____ the reclusive author to grant an interview; she had refused every request from journalists for over thirty years.
gre.clue: she had refused every request from journalists for over thirty years

en: An inappropriate expression or action; unhappiness
hook: IN-FELICITY: NOT FELICITOUS, not well chosen.
story: Infelicity. At his cousin's wedding, Farhan gave a toast praising the groom's loyalty, and then, meaning to be funny, mentioned the bride's former fiance. The room went silent. It was an infelicity: an inappropriate expression, a remark badly suited to the moment. Infelicity is literally the lack of felicity, which means both happiness and aptness of expression. So it can mean unhappiness, but the GRE usually means a clumsy phrase or misstep. Synonyms: gaffe, blunder, impropriety.

gre.s: The translation is generally elegant, yet one glaring ____ mars the final chapter: a solemn funeral oration rendered in breezy, comic slang.
gre.clue: a solemn funeral oration rendered in breezy, comic slang

en: Able to be understood
hook: INTELLIGIBLE: your INTELLIGENCE can grasp it.
story: Intelligible. Sabbir's grandfather in Chittagong speaks a dialect so thick that his Dhaka-born grandchildren catch barely half his words. Over a crackling phone line, he is hardly intelligible at all. But when Sabbir visits and listens face to face, the words grow clear. Intelligible means able to be understood. It shares a root with intelligent, but intelligent describes a mind, while intelligible describes a message. Opposite: unintelligible. Synonyms: comprehensible, clear, lucid.

gre.s: So badly damaged was the recording that the speaker's words were barely ____, and transcribers had to guess at nearly every sentence.
gre.clue: transcribers had to guess at nearly every sentence

en: Serving as a temporary substitute
hook: MAKESHIFT: MAKE do in a SHIFT.
story: Makeshift. When the cyclone shelter overflowed, families on the coast of Patuakhali built makeshift tents from old saris, bamboo poles, and plastic sheets. A school bench became a bed; an upturned bucket became a table. Everything was makeshift: serving as a temporary substitute until something better was available. The word comes from the old phrase to make shift, meaning to manage somehow with what you have. Synonyms: improvised, temporary, stopgap.

gre.s: Because the hospital had been destroyed by the earthquake, doctors treated patients in a ____ clinic set up in a school gymnasium until a permanent facility could be built.
gre.clue: until a permanent facility could be built

en: Former
hook: ONETIME: ONE TIME in the past.
story: Onetime. At a cricket coaching camp in Khulna, the boys noticed an old man quietly correcting their batting stances. Someone whispered that he was a onetime national team opener, famous back in the nineteen eighties. Onetime means former: what someone used to be. A onetime rival can become a friend; a onetime jute mill can become a shopping centre. Do not confuse it with one-time, meaning happening only once. Synonyms: former, erstwhile, previous.

gre.s: The senator, a ____ ally of the president, has become one of his fiercest critics since their bitter public quarrel over the budget last year.
gre.clue: has become one of his fiercest critics

en: Taking advantage of opportunities without regard to principles
hook: OPPORTUNISTIC: grabs every OPPORTUNITY, ethical or not.
story: Opportunistic. When a rumour of a salt shortage swept through Dhaka, a few traders hid their stock, then sold it at five times the usual price to panicking customers. They had not started the rumour, but they rushed to profit from it, with no regard for fairness. Their behaviour was opportunistic: grabbing every chance for gain, regardless of principle. In medicine, opportunistic infections strike when the immune system is weak. Synonyms: exploitative, unprincipled, expedient.

gre.s: Critics dismissed the politician's sudden embrace of environmental causes as ____, noting that he had opposed every green initiative until polls showed voters cared about them.
gre.clue: until polls showed voters cared about them

en: Seeming reasonable or probable
hook: PLAUSIBLE: deserves APPLAUSE for sounding right.
story: Plausible. Shuvo arrived at class forty minutes late. His first excuse, that a tiger had blocked the road in Mohammadpur, made everyone laugh. His second, that the bus had broken down near Asad Gate, was plausible: it seemed reasonable and likely to be true. The teacher accepted it. Note that plausible means believable, not necessarily true; a skilled liar tells a plausible story. Opposite: implausible, far-fetched. Synonyms: credible, believable, likely.

gre.s: Although the detective's theory was ____ enough to persuade the jury, later DNA evidence showed that the actual sequence of events had been quite different.
gre.clue: enough to persuade the jury

en: Behavior intended to impress or mislead
hook: POSTURING: striking a POSTURE (pose) for show.
story: Posturing. Before a local election, two candidates in Narsingdi held rallies on the same day. Each promised to build a bridge, a hospital, and a university by next year, and each pounded the podium. The voters smiled; they had heard it all before. It was mere posturing: behaviour meant to impress or mislead rather than to accomplish anything. A posture is the way you hold your body; posturing is striking a pose. Synonyms: grandstanding, bluster, affectation.

gre.s: Analysts dismissed the general's threats as mere ____, intended to impress his domestic audience rather than to signal any genuine intention of going to war.
gre.clue: intended to impress his domestic audience

en: Having great power or effect
hook: POTENT: full of POTENTIAL power.
story: Potent. Lamia's grandmother brewed a tea of ginger, black pepper, tulsi leaves, and honey whenever anyone caught a cold. One cup and your eyes watered; two, and the cough seemed to vanish. The remedy was potent: having great power or effect. Words can be potent too; a single photograph can become a potent symbol. Potent shares a root with potential and omnipotent, all meaning power. Opposite: impotent, weak. Synonyms: powerful, forceful, strong.

gre.s: Though the drug is administered in tiny doses, it is remarkably ____: a single milligram is enough to sedate a full-grown horse.
gre.clue: a single milligram is enough to sedate a full-grown horse

en: No longer needed; unnecessary repetition
hook: REDUNDANT: RE-DONE, repeated without need.
story: Redundant. Tanvir's first essay draft began: "In my personal opinion, I think that, in the end, the final result was a total success." His teacher circled almost every word. Personal, I think, in the end, final, total: all redundant, unnecessary repetition. Redundant also means no longer needed; in Britain, workers made redundant lose their jobs. Engineers, however, build redundant systems on purpose, as backups in case one part fails. Synonyms: superfluous, repetitive, unnecessary.

gre.s: Because the new software performs all of its checks automatically, the old manual inspections have become ____, and the company plans to eliminate them next year.
gre.clue: the company plans to eliminate them next year

en: Too important or sacred to be interfered with
hook: SACRO-SANCT: SACRED and SANCTIFIED.
story: Sacrosanct. In Kamal's family, Friday lunch is sacrosanct. Nobody schedules meetings, nobody travels, and even his busy surgeon aunt switches off her phone. Everyone eats together, whatever happens. Sacrosanct means too important or too sacred to be interfered with. It comes from the Latin sacer, holy, and sanctus, set apart. The word is often used with irony, as when a minister's favourite project is treated as sacrosanct. Synonyms: inviolable, untouchable, sacred.

gre.s: For decades the rule was considered ____, but the new director treated it as merely one tradition among many, open to revision like any other.
gre.clue: open to revision like any other

en: Showing sharp judgment, especially in practical matters
hook: SHREWD: sharp as a SHREW's teeth.
story: Shrewd. Anika's mother runs a small sari shop in Mirpur. When a big chain store opened nearby, she did not panic. She noticed that it closed at eight, so she began staying open until eleven, catching office workers on their way home. Her sales doubled. She is shrewd: showing sharp judgment, especially in practical matters like business. Shrewd once meant wicked; today it means clever and canny. Synonyms: astute, canny, sharp.

gre.s: A ____ investor, she sold her shares months before the crash, having recognized warning signs that most analysts had dismissed as insignificant.
gre.clue: having recognized warning signs that most analysts had dismissed

en: Plain; without decoration
hook: UN-ADORNED: not ADORNED.
story: Unadorned. Most buildings along one Gulshan avenue sparkle with glass and gold paint. But one small mosque stands apart: plain white walls, a simple wooden door, no decoration at all. Many visitors find it more beautiful than its neighbours. It is unadorned: plain, without decoration. To adorn is to decorate, and un means not. Writing can be unadorned too, simple and direct, like a good news report. Synonyms: plain, austere, unembellished.

gre.s: In contrast to the ornate, metaphor-laden style of his contemporaries, Hemingway wrote ____ prose, relying on short declarative sentences and everyday words.
gre.clue: In contrast to the ornate, metaphor-laden style of his contemporaries

en: Serving as a farewell
hook: VALEDICTORY: say VALE (farewell).
story: Valedictory. On the last day of the academic year, the oldest professor in the department gave one final lecture before retiring. He thanked his students, told stories from forty years in the classroom, and ended with two words: "Go well." It was a valedictory speech: serving as a farewell. In some countries, the top graduating student gives the valedictory address. From Latin vale, farewell, and dicere, to say: saying goodbye. Synonyms: farewell, parting.

gre.s: The retiring minister's ____ speech, delivered on her final day in parliament, graciously thanked even her fiercest opponents for decades of spirited debate.
gre.clue: delivered on her final day in parliament

en: Justified; having good reason
hook: WARRANTED: a WARRANT gives justification.
story: Warranted. When Nadia's landlord raised the rent by fifty percent, she complained to the building committee. They checked rates across the neighbourhood and found that no other flat had gone up by more than ten. Her complaint was warranted: justified, with good reason behind it. A warrant is an official justification, as in a search warrant. The opposite, unwarranted, means without justification, as in unwarranted criticism. Synonyms: justified, legitimate, merited.

gre.s: Given the company's long record of concealing defects, the regulators' skepticism about its latest safety claims seems entirely ____.
gre.clue: Given the company's long record of concealing defects

en: Having a feeling of vague or regretful longing
hook: WISTFUL: WISHFUL with a little sadness.
story: Wistful. Years after moving to Toronto, Imran found an old photograph of his school friends in Barishal, all grinning with muddy knees after a football match in the rain. He stared at it for a long time with a small, sad smile. His expression was wistful: full of vague, regretful longing for something past or out of reach. Wistful is gentler than grief; it is a soft ache. Synonyms: nostalgic, yearning, melancholy.

gre.s: Looking through photographs of the village where she grew up, the elderly novelist grew ____, longing for a world she knew had vanished forever.
gre.clue: longing for a world she knew had vanished forever
